title: The Great Purge, 1936-38

cards.b: Between 1936 and 1938 Stalin's secret police purged the Communist Party, the army and the state. Old Bolsheviks, generals and officials were tried in show trials, shot or sent to the Gulag. Historians still debate its causes and scale. Any honest account of communism in power must reckon with it.

cards.h: From Kirov to the show trials
cards.b: Sergei Kirov, the Leningrad party boss, was shot on 1 December 1934. Stalin used the killing to expand the security police's powers. The first Moscow show trial, in August 1936, convicted Zinoviev and Kamenev. Later trials in 1937 and 1938 took in Pyatakov, Radek, Bukharin and Rykov. Each confession was extracted under torture and followed by execution.

On 30 July 1937 the NKVD issued Order No. 00447. It targeted 'anti-Soviet elements' in set categories and fixed numbers for each region. Those in the first category were to be shot, and the second category sent to labour camps. Quotas turned arrests into a mass operation. Local officials often raised their own targets.

Nikolai Yezhov headed the NKVD from 1936 to 1938, and the period is known as the Yezhovshchina. Army commanders were arrested in 1937, including Marshal Tukhachevsky, who was shot in June. In late 1938 Lavrenty Beria replaced Yezhov, who was himself shot in 1940. The purges ended after the NKVD had been purged too.

NKVD records show about 1.5 million people arrested and about 680,000 shot in 1937-38. Those figures come from the archives, and historians such as J. Arch Getty have used them to measure the scale. Many more died in the camps or in exile. Exact totals are still debated, but the scale is not in doubt.

Robert Conquest's The Great Terror (1968) argued that Stalin's terror was the planned product of a totalitarian system, with the show trials staged from the top. Many older accounts follow this reading. It sees the purges as the logical outcome of Leninist dictatorship and single-party rule, a claim that critics of Marxism often make.

Getty's Origins of the Great Purges (1985) argued that local officials and the party's own disorder drove many of the arrests. He stressed the chaos of the bureaucracy and the local rush to meet quotas. Defenders of the totalitarian reading reply that the top set the quotas and the pattern. The debate asks how much of the terror was planned and how much was improvised.

Stalin's rule shaped how the CPI handled discipline. In the 1930s the party followed Comintern lines closely, and it was banned and its leaders jailed, as in the Meerut Conspiracy Case. After Khrushchev's 1956 speech, Indian communists debated Stalin's crimes. The 1964 split that created the CPI(M) was fought partly over the Soviet and Chinese lines, and it echoed the old question of how far loyalty to Moscow should go.

The Great Purge removed a generation of Bolshevik leaders. Stalin's victory meant that his line on the party, the state and the peasantry became the only one allowed. Khrushchev's 1956 secret speech, which attacked the 'cult of personality', was in part a reckoning with the purges. Its effects shaped the Soviet Union for the next thirty years.

Key takeaways

  1. The purges followed Kirov's murder in December 1934.
  2. Three Moscow show trials ran from 1936 to 1938.
  3. Order 00447 of 1937 set quotas for arrests and executions.
  4. Yezhov was replaced by Beria in late 1938.
  5. Historians debate planned terror against local disorder.
